title: Adjectives that are really verbs
title_target: គុណនាម ជា កិរិយាសព្ទ — kun-nie-niem chiè ke-re-yie-sap
goal: Describe people, things, and situations — and stop looking for an "is" that simply never goes before an adjective.
bekal: build adjective sentences with no linking word at all
know when ជា is used and when it isn't
negate adjectives with មិន … ទេ
use the intensifiers ណាស់, ខ្លាំង, ពេក, បន្តិច
describe people and things with thirty adjectives

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — Looking for a room to rent
dialogs.intro: Ani is looking for a place closer to her school. Notice that **not one** adjective sentence in this dialogue uses a linking word. "The room is big" is two words in Khmer, not four.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Adjectives ARE verbs — there is no "is"
body: This is the most important shift in thinking in the second half of the book. In Khmer, ធំ doesn't mean "big" but **"to be big"** — it is a full verb and can stand as a sentence on its own.

head: Khmer
Say it
Literally
Translation
rows: ខ្ញុំឃ្លាន
អាហារឆ្ងាញ់
ថ្ងៃនេះក្តៅ

after: ⚠️ Because adjectives are verbs, **they are negated like verbs**: មិន … ទេ. "I'm not hungry" is ខ្ញុំមិនឃ្លានទេ, not something with "isn't".
⚠️ And for the same reason, **ជា is never used before an adjective**. ខ្ញុំជាឃ្លាន is a classic English-speaker mistake, because we feel we need an "am" in there. You don't.
If it feels strange, think of headline English: "Room big, rent low." Khmer talks like this all the time, and it's perfectly correct. What you need to drop is the habit of inserting *am/is/are*.

grammars.title: When to use ជា, when not to
body: ជា (*chiè*) only links **two nouns**. If an adjective follows, it can't be there. At A1 this rule has no exceptions.

head: Sentence
Correct?
Why
rows: ខ្ញុំជាគ្រូ
ខ្ញុំជាជនជាតិឥណ្ឌូនេស៊ី
នេះជាបន្ទប់ខ្ញុំ
ខ្ញុំជាឃ្លាន
hungry = adjective → ខ្ញុំឃ្លាន
បន្ទប់ជាធំ
big = adjective → បន្ទប់ធំ
ថ្ងៃនេះជាក្តៅ
hot = adjective → ថ្ងៃនេះក្តៅ

after: A quick test: **if the next word can take "very" in front, it's an adjective — drop ជា.** "Very teacher" makes no sense, so ជាគ្រូ is right. "Very hungry" makes sense, so ជាឃ្លាន is wrong.

grammars.title: Stronger and weaker
body: These four little words set how strong the quality is, and they all go **after** the adjective — the opposite of English "very" and "a bit".

head: Word
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: ធំណាស់ — very big
ក្តៅខ្លាំង — really hot
ថ្លៃពេក — too expensive
ថ្លៃបន្តិច — a bit expensive
ធំល្មម — big enough
ឆ្ងាញ់ណាស់ណាស់ — incredibly delicious

after: ⚠️ They all go **after**, with no exceptions. ណាស់ធំ and ពេកថ្លៃ are wrong. This is one of the few places where the order is the reverse of English, so check it every time you build an adjective sentence.

rows: អស់កម្លាំង

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice **ចិត្តល្អ** — literally "heart good". ចិត្ត comes from the Sanskrit *citta* ("mind"), but here it means the heart as the seat of feelings. The pattern keeps recurring: **ចូលចិត្ត** (like) is literally "enter the heart", and **ចិត្តខូច** (heartbroken) is literally "heart broken", quite different from **ខឹង** (angry). Once you spot ចិត្ត, you'll find it in dozens of words.
